title: Edwin Hubble: The Redshift of the Running Galaxies
source_chapter: Chapter 5: Red-Shifts in the Spectra of Nebulae
authenticity_note: Drawn directly from Edwin Hubble's 1929 landmark PNAS paper 'A Relation between Distance and Radial Velocity among Extra-Galactic Nebulae' and his 1936 Silliman Lectures on cosmological redshift.
summary: Perched atop Mount Wilson in California with the 100-inch Hooker telescope, Edwin Hubble proved that fuzzy spirals in the sky were separate galaxies millions of light-years away, and that their light shifted toward the red end of the spectrum—proving the entire universe was born in a cosmic expansion.
content:
In the 1920s, most astronomers believed that our Milky Way galaxy was the entire cosmos—an isolated island universe floating in an infinite, timeless void.

Perched above the clouds at Mount Wilson Observatory in California, American astronomer Edwin Hubble stepped onto the observation platform of the 100-inch Hooker telescope—then the most powerful eye on Earth. In October 1923, Hubble photographed the spiral Andromeda nebula (M31). Examining the glass photographic plates under a magnifying loupe, he spotted a dim point of light that varied rhythmically in brightness.

It was a Cepheid variable star! Using Henrietta Leavitt's period-luminosity relation, Hubble calculated its distance. Andromeda was not a small gas cloud inside the Milky Way; it was nearly a million light-years away (now measured at 2.5 million)—a gigantic, independent galaxy containing hundreds of billions of stars! Overnight, the known universe expanded tenfold.

Hubble did not stop there. Collaborating with telescope technician Milton Humason, he gathered spectra from dozens of distant galaxies. Light from atoms leaves distinct dark fingerprint lines across the rainbow spectrum. But when Hubble inspected the spectral lines of distant galaxies, something bizarre stood out: the absorption lines were consistently shifted toward the longer, redder wavelengths—a phenomenon called redshift.

Even more astounding: the further away a galaxy was, the faster it appeared to be speeding away from us! In 1929, Hubble published his monumental law: velocity equals distance multiplied by a constant ($v = H_0 \cdot d$).

Galaxies were not merely flying through space; the fabric of space itself was stretching like the surface of an inflating balloon. If the universe was expanding outward, then winding time backward meant everything had originated from a single, intensely dense point—the Big Bang. Edwin Hubble had opened humanity's eyes to a dynamic, evolving cosmos.

stem_vocabulary.definition: The stretching of light wavelengths toward the red end of the spectrum as space itself expands.
The observation that galaxies are moving away from Earth at speeds proportional to their distance ($v = H_0 cdot d$).
A type of star that pulsates radially, varying in both diameter and temperature, used as a standard candle to measure cosmic distances.
The physical reality that the metric of space between galaxies is continuously increasing over time.
